notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0093.tlg001.1st1K-gr: ἔκτομον ('cut out') may instead be a separate name for the plant: 'some call the black [hellebore] ektomon, [or] Melampodion'. 'He' is Melampus, implied by Melampodion.
*Pharmakon* means both 'drug' and 'poison'; to 'be a drug' here is to take effect on the body as a drug or poison does.
*kynosbatos*: usually taken as the dog-rose, but its identity is uncertain. *klymenon*: not securely identified.
Sousa: apparently a cold place in Greece known for its hemlock, not Susa in Persia; not identified.

'Protective charms' renders *alexipharmaka*, literally 'things that ward off drugs (or spells)'. *tripolion*: not identified. *antirrhinon*: probably a snapdragon or weasel's-snout, though 'no root beneath' fits neither well.
*panakeia* ('all-heal'): not securely identified. Moly: an onion-like plant here; its identity, and its relation to Homer's moly, are uncertain.
*thēlyphonon*: a poisonous plant, perhaps a kind of aconite or leopard's-bane; identification uncertain. *agrōstis*: a creeping grass, perhaps couch grass.

nodes.text: Further, there are the things the drug-sellers and root-cutters say, some perhaps to the point, but others with theatrical exaggeration. For they bid one cut some [roots] standing with the wind [behind], as with certain others and with *thapsia* [deadly carrot], after anointing oneself with oil; for the body swells up if one stands facing [the wind]. With the wind [behind], too, [they say] one should gather the fruit of the *kynosbatos* [dog-rose?], or else there is danger to the eyes. Some [they say should be cut] by night, some by day, and some before the sun strikes [them], such as the plant called *klymenon*.

And there are many other such things. [They say] one should also draw a circle three times round the mandrake with a sword, and cut it facing west; and that a second man should dance round it in a circle and say as much as possible about sex. This seems similar to what is said about cumin, about the cursing when they sow it. One should also draw a circle round black hellebore and cut it standing facing east and praying; and watch out for an eagle both on the right and on the left; for there is danger for those cutting, if the eagle comes near, that they will die within the year. These things, then, seem to be additions, as has been said. But there are no methods of root-cutting besides those we have described.

Of the cyclamen, the root [is used] for bringing inflammations to suppuration, as a pessary for women, and, in honey, for sores; the juice, poured in [through the nose] with honey, for purging the head, and for making [people] drunk, if one steeps it in wine and gives it to drink. [They say] the root is also good as an amulet to speed childbirth, and for love charms. When they have dug it up, they burn it, then moisten it with wine and make it into lozenges, as with the [wine-]lees with which we clean ourselves.

Some call the black [hellebore] *ektomon Melampodion* (the 'cutting of Melampus'), since he was the first to cut and discover it. They also purify houses and flocks with it, chanting an incantation at the same time, and they use it for several other purposes as well.

XV. The places that seem richest in drugs are, among those outside Greece, especially those around Tyrrhenia and Latium, where they say Circe also lives; and even more, as Homer says, the region of Egypt. For he says Helen got from there 'fine [drugs], which Polydamna, wife of Thon, gave her, an Egyptian woman; there the grain-giving soil bears drugs in greatest number, many good when mixed, and many baneful.' Among these, he says, was that famous *nēpenthes* and *acholon* [banisher of grief and of anger], so as to produce forgetfulness and freedom from feeling one's troubles. And these [places], roughly, seem to have been pointed out, as it were, by the poets. For Aeschylus too, in his elegies, speaks of Tyrrhenia as rich in drugs: 'the Tyrrhenian race, a drug-making people.'

*Panakeia* [all-heal] grows in the rocky country around Psophis, both most abundant and best. Moly [grows] around Pheneus and on Cyllene. They say it is also like the one Homer spoke of, having a round root resembling an onion and a leaf like the squill; and that they use it for protective remedies and for magic; it is not, however, hard to dig up, as Homer says [it is].

Thrasyas of Mantinea had discovered, as he said, something of this kind, which made release [from life] easy and painless, using the juices of hemlock, poppy and other such plants, so that it was very compact and small, about a drachm's weight. It was entirely beyond remedy and able to keep for any length of time without changing at all. He took the hemlock not from wherever it happened [to grow], but from Sousa and any other place that was cold and shady; and the other [ingredients] likewise. He also compounded many other drugs, and from many [ingredients]. His pupil Alexias was also clever, and no less skilled than he; for he was experienced in the rest of medicine as well.

For it seems that some drugs are drugs [only] through lack of habituation, or perhaps it is truer to say that through habituation they are not drugs; for when the [body's] nature has accepted them and masters them, they are no longer drugs, as Thrasyas too used to say. For he said that the same thing is a drug for some and not a drug for others, distinguishing the natures of each; for he thought one ought to [do so], and he was skilled at discerning [them]. But clearly habit too does something, in addition to nature. At any rate Eudemus the drug-seller, who was highly regarded in his craft, having wagered that he would suffer nothing before sunset, ate a quite moderate amount, and could not contain it or master it.

*Thēlyphonon* ['female-killer'], which some call 'scorpion' because it has a root like a scorpion, kills the scorpion when scraped on [it]; and if one sprinkles white hellebore on [it], they say it comes back to life. It also kills cattle, sheep, draught animals and, in short, every four-footed animal on the same day, if the root or the leaves are put into the genitals; but it is useful against a scorpion's sting when drunk. It has a leaf like cyclamen, and a root, as was said, like a scorpion. It grows like *agrōstis* [couch grass] and has joints; it likes shady places. If what is said about the scorpion is true, then the other such things are also not incredible. And the fabulous tales too are not put together without reason.

But the following are sillier and less credible: the things said about amulets and in general about the so-called protective charms for bodies and for houses; and how they say that *tripolion*, according to Hesiod and Musaeus, is useful for every serious undertaking, which is why they dig it up by night after pitching a tent. So too, or even more so, with what is said about fame and good repute; for they say that the plant called *antirrhinon* [snapdragon?] produces fame. It is like cleavers, but has no root beneath, and its fruit has, as it were, a calf's nostrils. And [they say] that one anointed with it gains good repute.
